hook.support: Since 1993, TV election debates have had a line on the screen called the worm. It goes up when people like what they hear. It goes down when they don't. Does it pick the best argument?
hook.core: Since 1993, Australian TV has run a wiggly line across the bottom of the screen during election debates. It's called the worm. It goes up when a studio audience likes what they hear, and down when they don't. Leaders have learned to play to it. But does the worm reward the best argument, or just the best performance?

why.support: A debate has rules. Learn to listen, answer back with evidence, and stay calm. It helps in class, at work and in life.
why.core: A debate isn't a fight. It has rules: who speaks when, how long, and how you respond to the other side. Knowing the rules, listening closely, and answering with evidence will help you in class debates, team meetings, interviews and any time you need to stand your ground without losing it.
why.extend: Debate is structured disagreement. Its conventions (roles, timing, rebuttal and respectful questioning) let people test ideas without personal conflict. Active listening, evidence-based argument and clear linking of ideas are the skills that win debates, and they transfer directly to meetings, negotiations and interviews.

articles.title: How a debate works

body.support:
A **debate** is a contest between two teams. They argue about a **topic**. Topics start with *“That…”*.

**The teams.** The **affirmative** agrees with the topic. The **negative** disagrees. They take turns to speak.

**The rules.**

- A **chair** runs the debate.
- Each speaker has a time limit.
- No one interrupts.
- A judge picks the winner.

**Make a point.**

- Say your point.
- Give evidence: a fact or example.
- Explain why it matters.

**Listen.** While the other team talks, write down their points.

**Answer back.** Say: *“They said ___. **But** ___, **because** ___.”* That's a **rebuttal**.

Attack the idea, not the person.

**Good questions** are short: *“How do you know?”*
body.core:
A **debate** is a contest between two teams about a **topic**. Topics start with *“That…”*, like *“That phones should be banned at work.”*

**The teams.** The **affirmative** agrees with the topic. The **negative** disagrees. Each team usually has three speakers, and they take turns: affirmative, negative, affirmative, negative.

**The rules.** A **chair** runs the debate and calls each speaker. Speakers have a time limit. Nobody interrupts. You speak to the chair and the audience, not to the other team. An **adjudicator** (judge) decides who wins, usually on:

- **what** you said: your arguments and evidence
- **how** you said it: your voice, eye contact and confidence
- **how it fits together**: your structure and teamwork.

**Making an argument.** Use **point, evidence, explain**:

- **Point:** *“Our first argument is that a ban is unfair to workers with families.”*
- **Evidence:** a fact, example or expert.
- **Explain:** why it matters, and how it proves your side.

**Listening.** While the other team speaks, write down their main points. You can't answer what you didn't hear.

**Rebuttal.** This is where debates are won. Take their point, then show why it doesn't hold up:

*“They said ___. **But** ___, **because** ___. **So** ___.”*

Attack the **argument**, never the **person**.

**Questions.** In some debates and discussions, you can ask the other side questions. Good questions are short and fair: *“What evidence shows that?”* or *“How would that work for night-shift workers?”*

**Linking words** help listeners follow you: *firstly*, *furthermore*, *however*, *as a result*, *this shows that*.
body.extend:
A **debate** is a contest with rules between two teams. They argue about a **topic**, written as a statement: *“That phones should be banned at work.”*

**Roles and order.** The **affirmative** supports the topic; the **negative** opposes it. Teams usually have three speakers who alternate. The first speakers define the topic and set out each team's case. Middle speakers develop arguments. Final speakers focus on rebuttal and summary.

**Conventions.** A **chair** runs the debate and calls each speaker. Speeches are timed. In most school debates, you can't interrupt. Speakers talk to the chair and audience, not to the other team. An **adjudicator** judges:

- **matter:** the quality of arguments and evidence
- **manner:** delivery, including voice, eye contact and presence
- **method:** structure, responsiveness and teamwork.

**Building an argument.** Use **point, evidence, explain**: state a clear claim, support it with relevant evidence, and explain how it proves your case.

**Active listening.** Note the other team's arguments as they speak. Good rebuttal depends on hearing exactly what was said, not what you expected.

**Rebuttal.** Find a flaw, such as weak evidence, faulty reasoning or a missing view. Then respond: *“The negative claimed ___. **However**, ___, **because** ___. **Therefore** ___.”* Target the argument, never the speaker.

**Questioning.** Where the rules allow, short, fair questions can expose a weak point: *“What evidence supports that?”*

**Linking words** signal how ideas connect: *firstly*, *furthermore*, *however*, *as a result*, *this demonstrates*.

caseStudies.title: The worm

body.support:
In **1993**, two leaders had a TV debate before an election. Channel Nine added something new: **the worm**.

The worm was a line on the screen. It went up and down. It showed how a group of voters felt, second by second.

In **2007**, the people running the debate said: no worm. Channel Nine used it anyway. So they **cut** Nine's feed! Nine kept going using another network's feed.

In **2010**, the worm said Julia Gillard won, **63% to 37%**. But some newspaper writers said Tony Abbott won.

Who was right? The worm shows how people feel. A judge looks at the arguments and evidence. A good debater needs both.
body.core:
In **1993**, Prime Minister Paul Keating and Opposition Leader John Hewson faced off in a televised election debate. Channel Nine added something new: **the worm**.

The worm was a line across the bottom of the screen. It rose and fell with the live reactions of a studio group of **undecided voters**. Viewers at home could see, second by second, which lines worked and which fell flat.

The worm became a regular part of election debates. It also caused fights about the rules.

In **2007**, the **National Press Club** hosted the debate between John Howard and Kevin Rudd. Its rules said networks couldn't use the worm. Channel Nine used it anyway. During the debate, the feed to Nine was **cut**. Nine switched to another network's feed and kept the worm on screen.

By **2010**, the rule had been dropped. In the debate between Julia Gillard and Tony Abbott, Nine's worm gave Gillard a clear win, **63% to 37%**. But many newspaper commentators saw it as close, and some said Abbott won.

So who was right? The worm shows how an audience *feels*, moment by moment. It reacts to tone, confidence and attacks. An adjudicator looks at the whole case: the arguments, the evidence and the rebuttal.

A good debater needs to win both.
body.extend:
During the **1993** election campaign, Prime Minister Paul Keating and Opposition Leader John Hewson met in a televised debate. The Nine Network introduced a new feature: **the worm**.

The worm was a line that moved across the bottom of the screen, rising and falling with the real-time reactions of a studio group of **uncommitted voters**. Viewers could see which lines landed and which fell flat.

The worm became a fixture of election debates, and a source of conflict over the rules.

In **2007**, the **National Press Club** hosted the debate between John Howard and Kevin Rudd, under rules that barred networks from using the worm. Nine broadcast it anyway. Mid-debate, Nine's feed was **cut**. The network switched to another broadcaster's feed and kept the worm on screen.

By **2010** the restriction had been lifted. In the Gillard–Abbott debate, Nine's worm favoured Julia Gillard **63% to 37%**, yet many commentators judged the debate close, and some called it for Tony Abbott.

The gap reveals two ways of judging a debate. The worm measures moment-by-moment audience reaction, which responds strongly to tone, confidence and attack lines. An adjudicator weighs the whole case: the arguments, the evidence and the quality of rebuttal. Effective debaters aim to win on both.

**Topic:** That every Year 11 student should do work experience.

**My argument (affirmative)**
“Work experience shows you what a job is really like before you choose a course. My cousin was sure he wanted to be a chef. One week in a kitchen changed his mind, and it saved him a year of the wrong course.”

**Rebuttal**
“The negative said work experience takes time away from class. But one week is a small part of the school year, and what you learn can shape your whole pathway. That is time well spent.”

teacher.overview: Students learn the conventions of debate (topic, affirmative and negative, speaker order, the chair and adjudicator, time limits, no interruptions), how to build an argument (point, evidence, explain), how to listen and take notes on the opposition, how to rebut fairly (They said… But… because…), and how linking words connect ideas. They annotate a debate speech, sort fair and foul moves, write rebuttals on a flow sheet, and hold a class debate with a human worm. The case study is the TV worm: introduced by Channel Nine in 1993, cut from the 2007 debate feed for breaking the National Press Club's rules, and in 2010 favouring Julia Gillard 63% to 37% while many commentators judged it close.
prep: Choose two or three debate topics students care about (e.g. That phones should be banned at work; That the school week should be four days; That P-platers shouldn't carry passengers at night).
Make score cards 1 to 5 for the human worm.
Optional: play a short clip of a televised leaders' debate with the worm.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** the affirmative agrees with the topic; the negative disagrees. E.g. a chair runs it, time limits, no interrupting, speak to the chair, an adjudicator judges. They said ___. But ___, because ___. So ___.

**Speech:** 1 addressing the chair; 2 rebuttal; 3 team line; 4 point; 5 evidence; 6 linking words and conclusion.

**Sort:** rebuttal with evidence — fair; “only a kid” — foul; calling out — foul; clarifying question — fair; over time — foul; thanking — fair.

**Flow sheet (examples):** customers — but staff can be trained to keep phones away when serving, because the problem is when, not whether; only fair rule — but rules can be fair without a ban, because they apply to everyone equally; safety — but phones can be banned near machines only, because the risk is in that area.

**Case study:** the worm measured audience feeling moment by moment; it didn't measure evidence, logic or rebuttal. The Press Club may have worried it would distract viewers or pressure leaders. Answers will vary.

**Level Up (example):** Teenagers need more sleep. However, school starts early. As a result, students are tired, and this shows in how well they learn. Therefore, a later start would help.

realityCheck: **Students may think debating is posh.** Use topics from their world (work, cars, money, phones).
**Rebuttal is hard on the spot.** The flow sheet makes it concrete; let teams huddle for 30 seconds before rebutting.
**Keep it fair.** Stop any personal attacks immediately; it's the main lesson.
**The human worm is fun.** It also starts a great discussion about feelings versus arguments.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It prepares students for Have Your Say.
